opus-5.5.text:
I think the most honest way to put it is that language models right now are serving as the "common sense" layer for embodied intelligence, not yet as the thing that actually makes a robot move well.

If you look at what's happened over the last couple of years, the big contribution of language models has been on the high-level side. They give you task understanding, decomposition, some notion of world knowledge. If I tell a robot "clean up the table," a language model can reason that cups go to the sink, trash goes to the bin, that you probably shouldn't throw away the laptop. That kind of semantic prior used to be extremely hard to get, and now it's almost free. So in that sense, language models solved a problem that the robotics community had been stuck on for a long time.

But I'd be careful not to overstate it. Language is a very compressed, very human-centric abstraction of the world. It tells you *what* to do, but it says very little about *how* to do it physically: how much force to apply, how an object deforms, how contact evolves over a few hundred milliseconds. Those things are not really described in text anywhere on the internet. So when people build vision-language-action models by taking a pretrained language backbone and attaching an action head, what you often see is that the language part brings generalization in instruction following and object recognition, but the actual manipulation quality is still bottlenecked by physical data.

So my view is that the language model is currently more like a scaffold, or an interface. It's the interface between humans and the robot, and it's the scaffold that lets us bootstrap a large model architecture with a lot of prior knowledge. But I don't think language will be the core representation in the long run. The core representation for embodied intelligence should be something closer to the physical world itself: something that understands space, dynamics, and causality. That's why I'm quite interested in directions like world models, video generation, and 3D understanding, because those are trying to learn the structure of the physical world directly rather than through the bottleneck of text.

So to summarize: at this stage, language models are indispensable for understanding intent and providing semantic knowledge, but they're not sufficient. The harder, and I think more interesting, part of the problem is everything below language: perception, physical interaction, and learning from embodied experience. That's where most of the real progress still has to happen.

fable-5.1.text:
I think of the language model right now as the "brain" layer of embodied intelligence, but a very specific kind of brain — one that's very good at understanding and planning, and still quite weak at actually controlling a body.

Let me break that into two parts.

The first part is where language models genuinely changed the game. Before large models, a robot's "understanding" of the world was almost entirely hand-engineered. If you wanted a robot to clear a table, you wrote a pipeline: detect objects, classify them, define what "clear" means, specify the sequence. Every new task meant new engineering. What the language model brings is common sense and generalization. You can tell it "the guest is leaving, help them out," and it can infer that this probably involves fetching a coat, opening a door, maybe saying goodbye — without anyone ever having coded "guest leaving" as a scenario. That ability to decompose an open-ended human instruction into a sequence of sub-goals is enormously valuable, and it's the piece that was missing for decades.

The second part is where I'd be more cautious. The language model knows a great deal *about* the physical world, but it doesn't actually *experience* it. Everything it knows comes from text and images produced by humans. So it can tell you a cup is fragile, but it has no felt sense of how much force cracks it. It knows "pour the water" as a concept, but not the continuous, millisecond-level feedback loop of tilting a bottle while watching the level rise. That low-level control problem — perception to action in a closed loop, with physics in between — is not something language was ever designed to express. Humans don't describe how they walk; they just walk.

So at this stage I see the language model as the planner and the interface, and the actual motor intelligence still has to come from somewhere else — from vision-language-action models trained on real interaction data, from simulation, from large-scale demonstrations. The frontier right now is really about how these two layers connect. Do you keep them separate, with the language model issuing high-level commands to a lower-level policy? Or do you merge them into one end-to-end model that goes from pixels and words straight to joint torques? Both camps have serious people, and I don't think it's settled.

If I had to summarize: language models solved the "what should I do and why" problem surprisingly well. They haven't solved the "how do I actually do it with this body" problem. And the data bottleneck for that second problem is far more severe than it ever was for text, because the internet doesn't contain robot experience. That's the real constraint on the field right now — not model architecture, but where the embodied data is going to come from.

r001.rationale: The response says earlier systems required hand-engineered pipelines and that every new task required new engineering, conveying that fixed task encodings do not generalize to new tasks.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says language models bring “common sense and generalization” and can infer sub-goals for an open-ended instruction.

r003.rationale: The response presents generalization as a valuable contribution of language models, not as something outside embodied intelligence’s core focus at this stage.

astra-6.text:
I think, at this stage, language models are mainly providing a layer of semantic understanding and high-level reasoning for embodied intelligence. They can help a robot interpret what a person wants, break a task into steps, and draw on general knowledge about objects and situations.

But understanding a task in language and actually carrying it out are quite different things. If you ask a robot to bring you a glass of water, describing the steps is relatively easy. Perceiving the glass, grasping it with the right force, moving without spilling, and responding when something goes wrong require capabilities that language alone doesn’t provide.

So I see language models as an important component of a larger system. They need to work closely with perception, action, and feedback from the environment. The key question is how to ground their reasoning in what the robot can actually observe and do. A plan has to be tested through action, and the result has to inform the next decision. That connection is where much of the challenge lies.

r003.rationale: It discusses language models’ current role and the challenge of grounding plans in action, but does not judge that demand generalization is not the core focus of embodied intelligence at this stage.

sol-6.1.text:
I think, at this stage, language models are primarily a bridge between human intentions and an embodied system’s actions. They can help a robot understand an instruction, draw on general knowledge, and break a complex task into smaller steps. But understanding what someone asks is different from knowing how to carry it out in the physical world.

For example, if you ask a robot to bring you a glass of water, a language model can describe a reasonable sequence. The robot still needs to locate the glass, judge whether it can grasp it, handle its weight, and respond if something slips. Those capabilities require perception, action, and feedback from the environment.

So I see language models as an important component, especially for reasoning and communication, but not as the whole solution to embodied intelligence. The key is connecting their knowledge to physical experience, so that the system can act, observe what happened, and adjust its behavior. We should judge that integration by whether it helps the robot complete real tasks reliably.
